sources.outlet: Institute for Safe Medication Practices, QuarterWatch (2011 Q2)
sources.quote: A total of 4,237 reports from lawsuits targeted metoclopramide, a drug for reflux and other gastrointestinal disorders that can cause an often irreversible form of neurological damage
sources.searcher_note: Apr-Jun 2011 surge of lawsuit reports on metoclopramide; same page says these come from 'manufacturer legal departments' but names no maker. Names the drug, not Teva/Actavis/Mutual.

sources.outlet: Institute for Safe Medication Practices, QuarterWatch annual report (2011 Q3-Q4)
sources.quote: Table 2 (reprinted from the Executive Summary for reference) shows the drugs most frequently the target of personal injury lawsuits. Metoclopramide (REGLAN) led the 2011 rankings.
sources.searcher_note: Table 2 gives metoclopramide 11,450 lawyer-sourced report cases in 2011, first of all drugs; says such reports are filed by drug companies' legal departments. No maker named.

sources.outlet: American Journal of Gastroenterology (Ehrenpreis et al.), via Augusta University research profile
sources.quote: Only 3.6% of all FAERS reports but 70% of TD reports were filed by lawyers, suggesting a distortion in signal.
sources.searcher_note: Peer-reviewed study of lawyer-initiated metoclopramide FAERS reports, window 2004-2010 (before the 2011 surge). DOI 10.1038/ajg.2012.300 suggests online-first in 2012. No maker named.

sources.quote: They also looked at the example of the gut motility stimulator metoclopramide, of which they found 65% of the 27,918 metoclopramide reports received through 2018 were classified as LARs.
sources.searcher_note: FDA officials' Drug Safety letter: 65% of metoclopramide FAERS reports through 2018 are litigation-associated. Same page notes a prior study found lawyer reports did not meaningfully distort known signals (mild disagreement on impact, not on count).

sources.quote: A Pennsylvania-based watchdog group named Reglan and metoclopramide the most litigated drug in 2011, with over 11,000 litigation-related adverse event reports received by the FDA that year.
sources.searcher_note: Legal-marketing consumer site (date is page update). Page names Pliva, Actavis Elizabeth and Teva USA as lawsuit defendants, not as the filers of the FAERS reports.

sources.outlet: Health Science Reports (Chen et al.), full text via Europe PMC
sources.quote: This effect was particularly evident for metoclopramide, for which the number of dystonia reports declined markedly after exclusion, indicating that its reporting volume was largely driven by legal submissions
sources.searcher_note: 2026 FAERS dystonia study: metoclopramide report volume largely lawyer-driven. Pattern on the drug, no maker named.

notes: Every source found names the drug (metoclopramide/Reglan) and reports lawyer-sourced FAERS reports and a 2011 surge. None names Teva, Actavis or Mutual as the filers, and none has the 15,500 total, the 91% share or the 9,089 Apr-Sep 2011 count. ISMP (2011 Q2 and annual) says lawsuit reports come from manufacturers' legal departments, without naming firms. ISMP counts: 4,237 legal-case reports in Apr-Jun 2011; 11,450 for all of 2011. The AJG window is 2004-2010. Not fetchable: Drug Safety 2018 (s40264-018-0703-x) and FDA's Drug Safety 2019 letter (s40264-019-00834-1): Springer cookie loop, PubMed captcha. The RAPS piece covers the 2019 letter. Hauben & Harpaz, 'The Bidirectionality of Lawyer Reporting Bias in Disproportionality Analysis' (Drug Safety, July 2026; correction 2026-07-27) is post-cutoff but unreadable (Springer redirect, no abstract in Europe PMC), so it's unknown whether it mentions metoclopramide; not recorded. ISMP's HTML pages return 403; its PDFs load. Teva's FY2011 20-F search snippet mentioned about 2,000 metoclopramide product-liability suits, but the fetched text didn't show the paragraph, so it's not recorded.
